name: Soft Green
lede: Soft green is a descriptive phrase, not a fixed color: a light, gentle green, here a mid-bright leaf tone.

sections.title: A phrase, not a pigment
sections.body:
Books use *soft green* as plain description rather than as a name for one pigment or dye [1][2]. Paterson-style dictionaries do not list it, and the art books that use the phrase mean whatever mild green suits the sentence [1].

Three uses show the range. Gage writes of the soft greens and salmon pinks in a Hiroshige print that van Gogh heightened into bright complementary greens and reds [3]. A textile writer describes the soft green leaves on a silk shirt [4]. And the Pigment Compendium repeatedly calls minerals soft green, such as gerhardite and mitscherlichite, to describe their crystals [5]. In each case the phrase is loose description, not a defined hue [3][4][5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is a clear mid-light green. In our archive of 23,781 paintings only 2 hold it as a large enough patch, as photographed: an Indian portrait of the Emperor Jahangir (dated 1795) and a Robert Delaunay of 1914 [6]. Painters in this archive rarely used a green this fresh and light at full strength, so a match is rare indeed. Photographed paintings are aged and varnished, so the absence is partly the camera.
